qs.q: What is the very first step in the initiation of eukaryotic transcription by RNA Polymerase II?
o: Binding of TFIIH to unwind DNA
Phosphorylation of RNA Polymerase II by TFIIH
Binding of TBP within TFIID to the TATA box
qs.e: The binding of TBP (TATA-Binding Protein) within TFIID to the conserved TATA box is the first step in transcription initiation. TFIIH is involved later to unwind DNA and phosphorylate RNA Polymerase II.

qs.q: How does eukaryotic transcription fundamentally differ from prokaryotic transcription regarding enzyme requirements?
o: Eukaryotes use a single RNA polymerase without transcription factors
Prokaryotes require three distinct RNA polymerases and six GTFs
Eukaryotes require multiple distinct RNA polymerases and transcription factors
Prokaryotes require a complex set of general transcription factors
qs.e: Eukaryotic transcription is more complex, requiring three distinct RNA polymerases and multiple general transcription factors. Prokaryotic transcription uses a single RNA polymerase that does not require additional transcription factors.

qs.q: During the initiation of eukaryotic transcription, which specific component of the TFIID protein complex directly attaches to the TATA box?
qs.e: The TATA-binding protein is a special subunit inside TFIID that sticks to the TATA box. Transcription factor A joins the complex after TFIID has already bound.

ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Eukaryotic transcription converts DNA into RNA using three RNA polymerases and many transcription factors. It is tightly regulated, and its failure underlies many diseases.

sections.p: Transcription is the first step of gene expression, producing precursor RNAs that become mRNA, rRNA, or tRNA. Three RNA polymerases (I, II, III) handle different gene classes.
b: Pol III → 5S rRNA, tRNA, small RNAs

sections.p: RNA polymerase II binds the promoter with the help of general transcription factors (TFIID, TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, TFIIF, TFIIH). After initiation, the polymerase elongates the RNA chain and then terminates.
b: Promoter: TATA box, Inr, DPE motifs
CTD phosphorylation drives transition to elongation

t.b: Which transcription factors are bound to a promoter? Shows active or repressed regulation.

t.a: RNA polymerase II Ser2/Ser5 phosphorylation assay
t.b: Is Pol II in initiation or elongation phase? Guides interpretation of transcriptional block.

sections.p: Regulation occurs at chromatin level (histone modifications, DNA methylation), transcription factor availability, and RNA polymerase II CTD phosphorylation.

t.b: Is a promoter methylated? Hypermethylation may silence tumor suppressor genes.
Does inhibiting deacetylation reactivate transcription? Helps in certain cancers.

sections.p: Defects in transcription cause developmental disorders, cancers, and viral pathogenesis. Inhibitors like α‑amanitin block Pol II, leading to liver failure.
b: Mutations in TFIIH cause xeroderma pigmentosum
Pol II over‑activity drives oncogene over‑expression
Viral proteins (e.g., HIV Tat) hijack transcription

b: Pol I → rRNA, Pol II → mRNA, Pol III → tRNA/5S rRNA
CTD Ser5 phosphorylation = initiation; Ser2 = elongation
α‑amanitin = Pol II inhibitor → liver failure

whenToSeekHelp: Acute liver failure after mushroom ingestion (α‑amanitin poisoning)
Rapidly progressive neurological decline with known transcription factor mutation (e.g., xeroderma pigmentosum)
Unexplained severe cytopenias suggesting transcription‑driven bone‑marrow failure

faq.q: Why are there three RNA polymerases in eukaryotes?
faq.a: Each polymerase specializes for different gene types, allowing separate regulation of ribosomal, messenger, and transfer RNAs.

faq.q: How does α‑amanitin cause liver damage?
faq.a: It binds RNA polymerase II, halting mRNA synthesis, leading to loss of essential proteins and hepatocyte death.

faq.q: What is the clinical use of transcription‑targeted drugs?
faq.a: They can suppress oncogene expression or reactivate silenced tumor‑suppressor genes in cancers.
